etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English usage, from Anglo-Norman and Old French usage.

definitions.definition: A custom or established practice. [from 14th c.]

quote.citation: 1792, James Boswell, in Danziger & Brady (eds.), Boswell: The Great Biographer (Journals 1789–1795), Yale 1989, p. 170:
quote.text: [S]everal young people sung sacred music in the churchyard at night, which it seems is an usage here.

quote.citation: 1846 October 1 – 1848 April 1, Charles Dickens, Dombey and Son, London: Bradbury and Evans, […], published 1848, →OCLC:
quote.text: Mrs. Wickam, agreeably to the usage of some ladies in her condition, pursued  […]  the subject, without any compunction.

definitions.definition: The act of using something; use, employment. [from 14th c.]
The established custom of using language; the ways and contexts in which spoken and written words are used, especially by a certain group of people or in a certain region. [from 14th c.]
(now archaic) Action towards someone; treatment, especially in negative sense. [from 16th c.]

quote.citation: 1596, Edmund Spenser, “Book IV, Canto IV”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: Whose sharp provokement them incenst so sore, / That both were bent t'avenge his usage base  […]

quote.citation: 1693, [John Locke], “§115”, in Some Thoughts Concerning Education, London:  […]  A[wnsham] and J[ohn] Churchill, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Satisfy a child by a constant course of your care and kindness, that you perfectly love him, and he may by degrees be accustom'd to bear very painful and rough usage from you, without flinching or complaining
